result: P. vivax is the second most prevalent malaria pathogen with wider geographical distribution than P. falciparum, posing infection risk to 2.5 billion people, with 8.5 million clinical cases reported in 2016.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide epidemiological context for P. vivax malaria, all supported by appropriate citations (Howes et al., 2016; WHO 2017). These are established facts from the literature that provide background for the study.

result: P. vivax research is restricted to few laboratories with limited progress, and the quest for radical cure therapies is hindered by poor understanding of hypnozoite biology.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C26 establish the research gap and rationale for the study, supported by citations to Armistead and Adams, 2018. This provides appropriate justification for the work.

result: Tafenoquine was recently FDA-approved as a single-dose radical cure therapy for P. vivax, representing an improvement over 14-day primaquine regimen, but both drugs cannot be used in G6PD-deficient patients due to hemolysis risk, necessitating new drug development.
evaluation: Claims C7-C14 describe current treatment options and limitations, supported by appropriate citations (Frampton, 2018; Wells et al., 2010; Mazier et al., 2009). This establishes clinical need for the research.

result: Malaria transmission involves sporozoite invasion of hepatocytes and transformation to schizonts that release merozoites. P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. cynomolgi can form dormant hypnozoites that reactivate to cause relapse, responsible for 90% of relapsing malaria burden.
evaluation: Claims C15-C23 describe established malaria biology supported by appropriate citations (Prudêncio et al., 2011; Wells et al., 2010; Shanks and White, 2013; Adekunle et al., 2015). This provides necessary biological context.

result: P. cynomolgi, closely related to P. vivax, has been crucial for understanding hypnozoite biology and discovering liver-stage active compounds and anti-relapse drug candidates, despite recent advances in in vitro and in vivo models.
evaluation: Claims C24-C30 establish P. cynomolgi as an appropriate model system, supported by multiple citations. This justifies the choice of experimental system used in the study.

result: Transcriptomic analysis identified LISP2 (PcyM_0307500) as dramatically upregulated (72-fold) in P. cynomolgi schizonts but detectable (FPKM 12) in hypnozoites, with similar expression pattern in P. vivax.
evaluation: Claims C33-C42 describe the transcriptomic rationale for selecting LISP2, supported by citations to prior work (Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017; Cubi et al., 2017; Gural et al., 2018) and data analysis. The selection criteria and statistical significance (p=0.0009) are clearly stated.

result: LISP2 protein is 2038 aa (P. cynomolgi) and 2519 aa (P. vivax) with N-terminal signal peptide and conserved C-terminal 6-cys domain. Antibodies were raised against the 6-cys domain and validated by western blot.
evaluation: Claims C43-C49 describe protein structure and antibody generation, supported by sequence analysis, Figure 1A, and western blot validation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B). The methodological approach is sound and appropriately validated.

result: In P. cynomolgi, LISP2 expression first appears at day 3 in crescent-shape pattern in early trophozoites (LISP2+), becomes circular by day 4, and accumulates in peripheral vacuolar structures by day 5 in multinucleated schizonts (LISP2++), confirmed by IFA and FISH.
evaluation: Claims C50-C58 describe temporal and spatial LISP2 expression patterns supported by extensive IFA data (Figure 1B, supplements) and FISH validation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The progression is well-documented with multiple time points and complementary techniques.

result: In P. vivax in vivo, LISP2 expression pattern mirrors P. cynomolgi, with crescent staining at day 3 and a large fraction of LISP2- hypnozoites. LISP2 co-localizes with UIS4 at the PVM prominence in LISP2+ trophozoites.
evaluation: Claims C59-C66 demonstrate conservation of LISP2 expression in P. vivax in vivo (Figure 2A-B), validating findings from P. cynomolgi. Co-localization with UIS4 provides additional characterization. The in vivo validation strengthens the findings.

result: LISP2 is expressed in early developing liver stage parasites and represents a marker for initiation of liver stage schizogony in relapsing malaria species, discriminating between dormant hypnozoites and early developing parasites.
evaluation: Claims C67, C31, C148-C149 represent the primary conclusion about LISP2 as a developmental marker, supported by combined in vitro and in vivo data. This is the central finding of the manuscript.

result: At day 6, P. cynomolgi parasites segregate into three populations: 73% LISP2- hypnozoites (growing to ~6 μm by day 8-9), 4% LISP2+ trophozoites (constant ~6.9 μm), and 23% LISP2++ schizonts (growing to ~21.6 μm by day 10). LISP2- and LISP2+ parasites become indistinguishable by size after day 7-8.
evaluation: Claims C68-C77 provide detailed quantitative characterization of parasite populations supported by extensive measurements (Figure 3A-B, ≥90 cells per timepoint). The size kinetics data are robust with clear statistical reporting including percentiles.

result: Time course analysis shows LISP2- parasites persist as hypnozoites (≥65% from day 3-21), LISP2+ trophozoites peak at 15-20% on day 4 then remain ≤5%, and LISP2++ schizonts increase to ~20% from day 5-6 onwards.
evaluation: Claims C78-C83 describe population dynamics over 21 days supported by quantitative data from three independent experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The temporal dynamics are well-characterized with appropriate replication.

result: LISP2- parasites are transcriptionally active as shown by H3K9ac labeling, though schizonts are more active than hypnozoites based on number of H3K9ac-positive structures.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 demonstrate viability of LISP2- parasites using H3K9ac marker (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Video 1), supported by citations to prior work. This addresses potential concern about whether LISP2- parasites are viable.

result: PV1, a parasitophorous vacuole protein, localizes to the PV circumference and extensively co-localizes with LISP2 in LISP2++ schizonts, suggesting LISP2 is a PV resident protein.
evaluation: Claims C86-C90, C97-C99 describe LISP2/PV1 co-localization supported by extensive imaging (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Videos 2-5) and citations. The inference that LISP2 is a PV protein is reasonable but requires functional validation.

result: LISP2- hypnozoites and LISP2+ trophozoites are similar in size, both have functional PV (PV1/UIS4 positive), and can be distinguished by LISP2 expression. This provides an updated definition of hypnozoites as small, uni-nuclear persistent parasites with UIS4-prominence lacking LISP2.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93, C96, C117 synthesize characterization data to define hypnozoites molecularly. This is supported by combined size, PV marker, and LISP2 expression data. The definition is well-supported by the data presented.

result: The UIS4 prominence, initially regarded as a hypnozoite marker, is also present in small developing forms.
evaluation: Claims C94-C95 clarify prior understanding about UIS4, supported by citation to Gural et al., 2018 and confirmed in P. cynomolgi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This contextualizes why LISP2 is needed as an additional marker.

result: LISP2+ trophozoites observed throughout the time course show active transcription (H3K9ac+) and emerge after prophylactic drug treatment, strongly suggesting they result from hypnozoite activation/relapse rather than developmental arrest.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 provide evidence that LISP2+ parasites represent activating hypnozoites, supported by transcription data and drug treatment experiments. The inference is reasonable though the authors acknowledge they cannot entirely rule out arrested forms.

result: Drug treatment experiments show TQ (radical cure drug) kills all hepatic stages including LISP2- hypnozoites (70-83% reduction, p<0.05), while ATQ and KDU691 (prophylactic drugs) kill LISP2+ parasites at day 8 but LISP2+ parasites reappear by day 15-21, indicating hypnozoite reactivation.
evaluation: Claims C109-C129 demonstrate differential drug susceptibility with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 4A-C). The experimental design with drug washout and extended monitoring provides strong evidence for hypnozoite reactivation. Sample sizes and p-values are reported.

result: Dose-response experiments show LISP2+ parasites are 13-14 fold more susceptible to ATQ (IC50: 0.036 vs 0.48 μM) and KDU691 (IC50: 0.13 vs 1.8 μM) than LISP2- parasites, while TQ shows similar activity against both populations.
evaluation: Claims C130-C132, C141-C144 provide quantitative IC50 values from dose-response curves (Figure 4D) with three independent biological replicates. The differential susceptibility strongly supports the hypnozoite identity of LISP2- parasites.

result: LISP2- parasites fulfill pharmacological criteria for dormant hypnozoites: susceptibility to 8-aminoquinolines (TQ) but phenotypic resistance to atovaquone and PI4K inhibitors, along with appropriate morphological characteristics.
evaluation: Claims C133-C135, C113-C114 synthesize drug susceptibility and morphological data to validate LISP2- parasites as hypnozoites. This is well-supported by the combined drug treatment and characterization experiments.

result: All tested drugs (TQ, KDU691, ATQ, PQ) were non-cytotoxic to simian hepatocytes up to 10 μM.
evaluation: Claim C145 demonstrates drug effects are parasite-specific, not due to hepatocyte toxicity, supported by CCK-8 viability assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This is an important control.

result: LISP2 can assess anti-relapse drug activities in vitro, with prophylactic drugs selectively killing LISP2+ parasites while LISP2- hypnozoites are only sensitive to tafenoquine, making LISP2 suitable for drug discovery assays.
evaluation: Claims C32, C146-C147, C150 demonstrate proof-of-concept for LISP2 as a tool for drug screening, supported by differential drug susceptibility experiments. This represents a practical application of the findings.

result: LISP2 expression closely coincides with the beginning of liver-stage development and is a marker of malaria relapse, providing a powerful tool to distinguish dormant from activated hypnozoites in drug assays.
evaluation: Claims C115, C107, C140 represent the main conclusions, supported by combined temporal expression, drug susceptibility, and reactivation data. This synthesizes the key findings of the manuscript.

result: Sporozoite inoculum size critically influences relapse rate in simian P. cynomolgi malaria.
evaluation: Claim C106 acknowledges a limitation regarding clinical relevance, supported by citation to Schmidt, 1986. This is an appropriate caveat about extrapolating to clinical relapse rates.

result: PV1 interacts with export machinery in blood stages, but functional studies are needed to determine if LISP2 and PV1 play similar roles in liver stages.
evaluation: Claims C100-C101 cite prior work on PV1 function and appropriately note that functional studies are needed for liver stages. This is a reasonable speculation for future work.

result: Future work with GFP-expressing parasites and novel in vitro assays measuring LISP2 activation will further establish the developmental sequence and enable anti-relapse drug screening.
evaluation: Claims C108, C116 describe future work and potential applications. While reasonable based on the findings, these are speculative and not demonstrated in the current study.

result: Discovery of radical cure drugs (preventing relapse and eliminating all liver stages including hypnozoites) remains challenging due to lack of high-throughput screening assays and tractable markers for hypnozoite reactivation.
evaluation: Claims C136-C139 establish the drug discovery challenge and need for the work, supported by citation to Campo et al., 2015. This provides rationale for the practical application of LISP2.
